mainTopic: Half-slaves and slaves missing only their גט שחרור: who gets the קנס and payments, eating תרומה, and selling the future קנס
overview: The amud opens by challenging a ברייתא. When an ox kills a half-slave, half-free person, the ברייתא splits the payment instead of going by whose day it was. The גמרא answers that death is different, because the person himself is gone for good. A temporary injury, like a withered hand that will heal, follows the 'whose day' rule. That example fits אביי but troubles רבא, and the גמרא offers two ways to answer for רבא. Next comes a new question: does a slave who is free in practice but still missing his גט שחרור bring the thirty-shekel קנס to his master? Two proofs are tried and pushed off, and along the way we see a dispute over whether a slave freed by losing a limb needs a גט at all. A parallel question asks whether such a slave may eat תרומה, and the proof from רב משרשיא's mixed-up babies is rejected. Finally the גמרא asks whether a master can sell just the future קנס for his slave, and explains why even רבי מאיר might not allow it.

steps.title: Why split the payment instead of going by whose day it was?
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא says that when an ox kills a half-slave, the master gets half the קנס and the heirs get half the כופר. The גמרא asks why we don't use the 'whose day' rule here.
steps.simpleTranslation: '...and half a ransom goes to his heirs.' Why? Let us say here too: if it happened on the master's day, the payment goes to the master; if it happened on his own day, it goes to himself!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes quoting a ברייתא about an ox killing a half-slave and then challenges it. Earlier it taught that payments for such a person go by whose day it was, so why split the payment here?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier, the rule for someone who injures a half-slave was: on the master's day, pay the master; on the slave's own day, pay the slave. The ברייתא instead splits the death payment in half, with half a קנס (the 30 שקלים for a slave) to the master and half a כופר to the heirs. The challenge is that the 'whose day' rule should apply here too.

keyTerms.meaning: Ransom: the payment an ox owner makes when his ox kills a free person
Heirs
Why?
The master's day, when the half-slave works for the master
His own day, when the half-slave works for himself

phrases.english: and half a ransom to his heirs.
Why?
Let us say here too:
the master's day goes to his master,
his own day goes to himself!
phrases.notes: Here 'himself' means his heirs, since he has died.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the ברייתא, using the 'whose day' rule taught just before this section.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's ruling that the death payment is split between the master and the heirs
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If injury payments go by whose day it was, death payments should also go entirely to whoever 'owned' that day.

steps.title: Death is different because the principal is gone
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that death is different: the whole person, the 'principal', is gone, so the master loses his share permanently no matter which day it was.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is different here, because the principal is used up.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. When the person dies, the master's half of him is lost forever, so the 'whose day' rule doesn't fit.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The 'whose day' rule works only for a temporary loss, where the question is whose working time was lost. Death destroys the person himself, and each partner (the master's half and the free half) loses his share for good. So each side is paid for its half, no matter which day it happened.

keyTerms.meaning: It is different here
The principal is used up: the core asset itself is destroyed

phrases.english: It is different here,
because the principal is used up.
phrases.notes: 'Principal' means the person himself. He is gone for good, not just missing some work days.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 1.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing the case: a permanent loss versus a temporary loss
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The 'whose day' rule should apply to every payment, including death.
steps.terutzMaskana: The 'whose day' rule applies only when the principal is not destroyed; death destroys it, so the payment is split.

steps.title: Then when does the 'whose day' rule apply?
steps.stepSummary: If death is excluded, the גמרא asks what case of an ox injuring a half-slave would follow the 'whose day' rule.
steps.simpleTranslation: But then, what is the case where the principal is not used up?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא follows up on its answer. It asks for an example where the injury does not destroy the principal, so that the 'whose day' rule would apply.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 2 limited the 'whose day' rule to cases where the person is not permanently lost. Now the גמרא wants a concrete case with an ox where that is true.

keyTerms.meaning: But then / rather
What is the case? What does it look like?

phrases.english: But then, what is the case
where the principal is not used up?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on the answer in step 2 by asking for the opposite kind of case.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A case of an ox injuring a half-slave where the loss is only temporary, so the 'whose day' rule applies

steps.title: A withered hand that will heal
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא's example: the ox struck his hand, the hand withered, but it will heal.
steps.simpleTranslation: Such as where it struck him on his hand, and his hand withered, but it will eventually return to normal.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers its own question. A hand that is paralyzed for now but will heal is a temporary loss, so the payment goes by whose day it was.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Because the hand will recover, the person keeps his full value in the long run. Only time is lost, which fits the 'whose day' rule.

keyTerms.meaning: Such as / for example
His hand withered (became paralyzed)
It will eventually return (heal)

phrases.english: Such as where it struck him on his hand,
and his hand withered,
and it will eventually return.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 3.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: An injury causing temporary paralysis of the hand, which will heal

steps.title: The case works for אביי but not for רבא
steps.stepSummary: The withered-hand case fits אביי, who has the injurer pay both the big and the small loss-of-work payments. For רבא only daily lost work is paid, and an ox owner never pays for lost work, so the case seems to have no payment at all.
steps.simpleTranslation: This works well for אביי, who says: he pays him the big loss-of-work payment and the small loss-of-work payment. That is fine. But according to רבא, who says he pays only for each day's lost work, there is a problem: this is an ox, and an ox owner pays only for damage!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tests the withered-hand answer against two views. It fits אביי, but it seems to fail for רבא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For a temporary injury, אביי requires a 'big' payment for the drop in market value and a 'small' payment for the actual days lost, so there is a real payment that an ox owner can owe. רבא holds that only the daily lost work (שבת) is paid. Since an ox owner pays only נזק and never שבת, under רבא nothing is owed in this case, and the example doesn't work.

keyTerms.meaning: This works well (for one view)
Big loss-of-work payment: the drop in his value as if sold
Small loss-of-work payment: wages for the days actually lost
His lost work of each and every day
Damage: the loss in the injured person's value

steps.confusionAlert: Even though אביי and רבא are discussing human injurers, the problem here is the ox. An ox owner pays only for נזק and never for שבת (lost work), so under רבא nothing is left to divide.
steps.whyThisMatters: This connects our case to the famous argument between אביי and רבא about how to pay for a temporary injury, and it sets up the need for a better answer for רבא.

phrases.english: This works well for Abaye, who says:
he gives him the big loss-of-work payment,
phrases.notes: This is how much less he would sell for in the slave market because of the injury.

phrases.english: and the small loss-of-work payment. That's fine.
But according to Rava, who says:
he gives him only
his lost work for each and every day;
this is an ox,
and an ox pays only damage!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the withered-hand example from step 4 by checking it against רבא's view.
steps.kashyaTarget: The withered-hand example as a case of the 'whose day' rule with an ox
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: For רבא a temporary injury is paid only as daily lost work, which an ox owner never pays. So there is no payment to split by day.

steps.title: The withered hand was caused by a person, not an ox
steps.stepSummary: First answer: the withered-hand case is about a person who struck the slave, and a person does pay for lost work.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you want, say that the case is where a person struck him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the problem from Step 5. It says the withered-hand case is not about an ox at all. A person struck the slave.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The problem was that for רבא, an ox owner never pays for lost work, so the withered-hand case had no payment to split by days. A person who injures does pay for lost work (שבת). So there is a real payment, and the 'whose day' rule decides who gets it.

keyTerms.meaning: If you wish, say (introduces one possible answer)
When a person struck him

phrases.english: If you wish, say:
when a person struck him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of Step 5 by changing who caused the injury.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining the case (person instead of ox)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The withered-hand case is about an ox, which for רבא leaves no payment at all.
steps.terutzMaskana: The case is about a person who struck him, who does pay for lost work, so the 'whose day' rule has something to apply to.

steps.title: רבא does not accept that statement
steps.stepSummary: Second answer: the rule that payment goes by whose day it was is just an amoraic statement, and רבא does not have to agree with it.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you want, say: it is a statement of an אמורא, and רבא does not agree with that statement.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second, different answer. The rule that the payment goes by whose day it was is not from a משנה or ברייתא, only from an אמורא, so רבא can disagree with it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first answer kept the rule and changed the case to a person striking him. This answer keeps the case as an ox but says the rule of dividing the payment by days is just one אמורא's view, which רבא does not share. Since an אמורא can disagree with another אמורא, the question against רבא falls away.

keyTerms.meaning: A statement of an אמורא (not a משנה or ברייתא)
He does not hold of it, he disagrees

phrases.english: And if you wish, say:
It is a statement [of an amora],
and Rava does not hold of that statement.
phrases.notes: "That statement" is the אמורא's rule that payment for injuring a half-slave goes by whose day it was.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second, separate answer to the קשיא of Step 5.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rejecting the authority of the source for this opinion
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The withered-hand example is binding on everyone, so it must fit רבא.
steps.terutzMaskana: The 'whose day' payment rule is only an amoraic statement; רבא is free to disagree with it.
steps.whatToRemember: Two ways to save רבא: either the injurer was a person (who pays for lost work), or רבא simply rejects that אמורא's 'whose day' rule.

steps.title: Does a slave waiting only for his document of freedom bring a fine?
steps.stepSummary: New question: if an ox kills a slave who is only missing his גט שחרור, does the master still get the thirty-shekel קנס?
steps.simpleTranslation: They asked: a slave who is held back only by a document of freedom, does he bring a fine or not? The תורה says, "Thirty shekels of silver he shall give to his master" — and this person is not really a master. Or maybe, since the slave is still missing his document of freedom, we still call him a master?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new question. A slave is free in practice but has not yet received his גט שחרור; if an ox kills him, does the master get the קנס?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק gives the thirty shekels "to his master." One side: this person no longer acts as a master, so no קנס. Other side: as long as the document has not been given, he is still legally called a master, so he gets the קנס.

keyTerms.meaning: A question was asked (an open question the גמרא tries to answer)
Held back only by a document of freedom; free in practice but missing the document
A fixed fine; here, the thirty shekels paid for a slave
Master
The Merciful One, meaning the Torah

phrases.english: A question was asked of them:
One held back only by a document of freedom,
does he have a fine
or does he not have a fine?
"Thirty shekels of silver he shall give to his master"
the Merciful One said —
and this one is not a master,
or perhaps
since he is lacking a document of freedom,
we call him a master?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new question, related to the half-slave topic but separate from the 'whose day' discussion.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether a master who only still owes the slave his document of freedom counts as "his master" for the thirty-shekel קנס.
steps.whyThisMatters: It asks what makes someone a master: real control and work, or the formal legal status until the document is given.

steps.title: Trying to prove it from the half-slave ברייתא
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא tries to prove the master does get the קנס, from the ברייתא that gives half the קנס to the master of a half-slave, read according to the משנה אחרונה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: if an ox killed someone who is half slave and half free, the owner gives half the fine to his master and half the ransom to his heirs. Isn't this according to the later משנה?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings the ברייתא from Step 1 to answer the new question. It suggests the ברייתא follows the משנה אחרונה, where the master must free the half-slave.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the משנה אחרונה, בית הלל agreed with בית שמאי that the master is forced to free the half-slave. So that half-slave is really just waiting for his גט שחרור. Yet the ברייתא still gives the master half the קנס, which would prove that a master in this situation does get the קנס.

keyTerms.meaning: Come and hear (introduces a proof)
Half slave and half free
Ransom payment, here paid to the heirs
The later version of the משנה, after בית הלל changed their view

steps.confusionAlert: This is not a new ברייתא. It is the same ברייתא from Step 1, now used to answer a different question.

phrases.english: Come and hear:

phrases.aramaic: הֵמִית מִי שֶׁחֶצְיוֹ עֶבֶד וְחֶצְיוֹ בֶּן חוֹרִין –
phrases.english: [If an ox] killed one who is half slave and half free —
he gives half the fine to his master
and half the ransom to his heirs.
What, is it not according to the later Mishnah?
phrases.notes: In the later version, the master is forced to free him, so he is really just missing his document.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע: הֵמִית מִי שֶׁחֶצְיוֹ עֶבֶד וְחֶצְיוֹ בֶּן חוֹרִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tries to answer the question of Step 8 using the ברייתא from Step 1.
steps.raayaObject: That a master whose slave is only missing his גט שחרור still receives the קנס.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא giving half the קנס to the master of a half-slave, read according to the משנה אחרונה, where the master is forced to free him.

steps.title: The half-slave source follows the earlier version of the משנה
steps.stepSummary: The proof from step 9 is rejected. The ברייתא about half the קנס follows the משנה ראשונה, where a half-slave remains a real half-slave.
steps.simpleTranslation: No. That ברייתא follows the משנה ראשונה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the proof from step 9. It says the ברייתא about a half-slave follows the earlier version of the משנה, not the later one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The proof only worked if the half-slave was already supposed to be freed, so that he was 'just missing a גט'. In the משנה ראשונה he works alternate days for himself and for his master, so he is a real half-slave. That is why his master gets half the קנס, and it teaches nothing about a slave who is only missing his גט שחרור.

keyTerms.meaning: The earlier version of the משנה, before it was changed
The later, revised version of the משנה

phrases.english: No, it follows the first version of the משנה.
phrases.notes: In that first version, the half-slave keeps working for his master every other day, so he is still truly half a slave.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof brought in step 9
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the proof that a slave missing only his גט שחרור still brings a קנס to his master
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The proof assumed the ברייתא follows the משנה אחרונה. It can follow the משנה ראשונה, where the half-slave is genuinely half a slave.

steps.title: Proof from the master who knocked out a tooth and then blinded an eye
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא says the master pays the slave for the eye. This suggests a slave missing only his גט is treated as free, so the master gets no קנס.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: if a master knocked out his slave's tooth and then blinded his eye, the slave goes free because of the tooth, and the master pays him the value of the eye. If you say a slave missing only his גט does bring a קנס, and that קנס goes to his master, there is a problem. If other people injured him, they would pay his master. Now that the master himself injured him, would the master pay the slave?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new proof, this time pointing the other way: that the master does NOT get the קנס. It uses a ברייתא about a master who injured his slave twice.
steps.deeperAnalysis: After the tooth is knocked out, the slave has earned his freedom but has not yet received his גט. Even so, the master must pay him for the eye, as if he were a free man. If such a slave were still treated as his master's property for payments like the קנס, then money for injuring him would belong to the master, and the master would be paying himself.

keyTerms.meaning: Come and hear: the גמרא is bringing a source as proof
The slave goes free because of his tooth (שמות 21:27)
The value of his eye, meaning payment for the injury
A fixed penalty; here, the thirty shekels paid when an ox kills a slave

phrases.english: Come and hear:

phrases.aramaic: הִפִּיל אֶת שִׁינּוֹ וְסִימָא אֶת עֵינוֹ –
phrases.english: If the master knocked out his slave's tooth and then blinded his eye,
he goes free because of his tooth,
and the master gives him the value of his eye.
And if you say such a slave does bring a קנס,
and the קנס goes to his master,
then now, if others injured him,
they would give the payment to his master;
so if his master himself injured him,
would he give the payment to the slave?!

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע: הִפִּיל אֶת שִׁינּוֹ וְסִימָא אֶת עֵינוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the proof that the master gets the קנס was rejected, the גמרא tries a proof that he does not
steps.raayaObject: That a slave missing only his גט שחרור does not bring a קנס to his master
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא of a master who knocked out his slave's tooth and then blinded his eye, and pays the slave for the eye

steps.title: That ברייתא may hold that no גט is needed at all
steps.stepSummary: The proof is rejected. The tooth-and-eye ברייתא may follow the view that a slave freed by losing a limb needs no גט, so he is already fully free. The גמרא quotes the ברייתא with that dispute.
steps.simpleTranslation: Perhaps that ברייתא follows the one who says no גט is needed. As a ברייתא teaches: for all of these injuries, a slave goes free through them, and he needs a גט שחרור from his master; these are the words of רבי ישמעאל. רבי מאיר says: he does not need one. רבי אליעזר says: he needs one. רבי טרפון says: he does not need one. רבי עקיבא says: he needs one.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the proof from step 11. It quotes a ברייתא showing that תנאים argue about whether such a slave even needs a גט שחרור.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Our question is about a slave who still needs a גט. If the tooth-and-eye ברייתא follows a תנא who holds that losing a tooth frees the slave on the spot, then by the time of the eye he is completely free. That would explain why the master pays him, and it proves nothing about a slave still waiting for his גט.

keyTerms.meaning: Perhaps: a typical word for pushing off a proof
According to the one who says
A document of freedom that a master gives a slave
He does not need it, meaning he goes free automatically

steps.confusionAlert: All these תנאים agree the slave goes free. They only argue about whether he also needs a written גט שחרור to finish the process.

phrases.english: Perhaps it follows the one who says he does not need a גט,
as a ברייתא teaches: with all of them,
phrases.notes: "All of them" means all the body parts whose loss sets a slave free.

phrases.english: a slave goes out to freedom through them,
and he needs a גט שחרור from his master,
these are the words of רבי ישמעאל.
רבי מאיר says: he does not need one.
רבי אליעזר says: he needs one.
רבי טרפון says: he does not need one.
רבי עקיבא says: he needs one.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof brought in step 11
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the proof that a slave missing only his גט brings no קנס to his master
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The ברייתא may follow a תנא who holds that losing a tooth frees the slave without any גט. Then he is fully free when the master blinds his eye, which is not our case.

steps.title: The compromise ruling: tooth and eye differ from other limbs
steps.stepSummary: The מכריעין rule like רבי טרפון (no גט needed) for tooth and eye, because the תורה gave the freedom. They rule like רבי עקיבא (a גט is needed) for other limbs, because that freedom is a rabbinic penalty.
steps.simpleTranslation: Those who decide between the views before the חכמים say: The words of רבי טרפון seem right for a tooth and an eye, since the תורה granted him his freedom. The words of רבי עקיבא seem right for the other limbs, since that is a penalty set by the חכמים.
steps.whatsHappening: This is the end of the ברייתא the גמרא quoted. A group of decisors offers a middle position between the two sides of the dispute.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For a tooth or an eye, the תורה itself frees the slave, so he goes free on his own without a גט. For the other limbs, the slave's freedom is a penalty the חכמים placed on the master, so the master must still write a גט. Notice that the tooth-and-eye ברייתא from step 11 deals exactly with a tooth, where by this view no גט is needed.

keyTerms.meaning: Those who decide between opposing views by finding a middle ground
Granted it to him, meaning gave him his freedom
The other limbs and body parts
A penalty made by the חכמים, not written in the Torah

steps.whatToRemember: For a slave freed by injury, tooth and eye (from the תורה) free him without a גט according to the מכריעין. Other limbs (a rabbinic penalty) still need a גט. Both proofs about the קנס for a slave missing only his גט have been rejected so far.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows the key idea behind the dispute: freedom that comes straight from the תורה takes effect by itself, while freedom created by a rabbinic penalty still needs the master to act.

phrases.english: Those who decide before the חכמים say:
The words of רבי טרפון seem right
for a tooth and an eye,
since the Torah granted him his freedom,
and the words of רבי עקיבא seem right for the other limbs,
since it is a penalty set by the חכמים.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the ברייתא quoted in step 12 with a compromise ruling
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A slave freed through his tooth or eye needs no גט שחרור because the Torah freed him. A slave freed through other limbs needs a גט because that freedom is a rabbinic penalty.

steps.title: How can the other limbs be called a penalty?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the word קנס used in step 13. The rule about the other limbs comes from learning פסוקים, so it is not just a rabbinic penalty.
steps.simpleTranslation: A penalty?! But we learn it from the verses!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the reason given in step 13 for siding with רבי עקיבא on the other limbs. That reason was that their freedom is only a rabbinic קנס.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 13 said the other limbs are different from tooth and eye because their freedom is a קנס of the רבנן. But we know the other limbs free a slave because we learn them out of the פסוקים about tooth and eye. So calling it a קנס seems wrong.

keyTerms.meaning: A penalty
Verses (פסוקים)
We learn out (from a פסוק)

phrases.english: A penalty?!
But we learn it from the verses!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the reason given in step 13
steps.kashyaTarget: The word קנס used for the other limbs
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Something learned from פסוקים cannot be called a rabbinic penalty.

steps.title: Fixing the reason: it is a מדרש חכמים
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא changes the wording. The other limbs are different because their source is a מדרש חכמים, not an open פסוק.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, say: since it is a teaching of the חכמים.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by fixing the wording of the reason. It does not drop the reason.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The other limbs are not written openly in the תורה. The חכמים learn them out from the פסוקים. That is why they can be treated as weaker than tooth and eye, so a גט is still needed for them. The word 'penalty' is swapped for 'a teaching of the חכמים.'

keyTerms.meaning: Say (read it this way instead)
Something the Sages learn out of the פסוקים, not written openly

phrases.english: Rather, say:
since it is a teaching of the Sages.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא אֵימָא: הוֹאִיל וּמִדְרַשׁ חֲכָמִים הוּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 14
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The other limbs were called a rabbinic קנס.
steps.terutzMaskana: The other limbs are a מדרש חכמים, so they are weaker than tooth and eye, which are written openly.
steps.whatToRemember: Tooth and eye are written openly in the תורה, so no גט is needed. The other limbs come from a מדרש חכמים, so a גט is needed. With both proofs pushed off, the question from step 8 (whether a slave missing only his גט שחרור brings a קנס) is left unanswered.

steps.title: Does a slave missing only his release document eat תרומה?
steps.stepSummary: A new question is asked. A כהן's slave is really free, but he has not yet received his גט שחרור. May he still eat תרומה?
steps.simpleTranslation: They asked: a slave who is held back only for lack of a release document, does he eat תרומה or not? The תורה says 'the purchase of his money,' and this slave is not the purchase of his money. Or perhaps, since he still lacks a release document, we do call him 'the purchase of his money'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new question about a slave who is only waiting for his גט שחרור. Is he still the כהן's slave for eating תרומה?
steps.deeperAnalysis: A כהן's slave may eat תרומה because the פסוק calls him 'קנין כספו', the purchase of his money. One side says the master can no longer make him work, so he is not really 'purchased' anymore. The other side says that as long as he lacks the גט, he still counts as the master's purchase.

keyTerms.meaning: They asked (a question with no clear answer yet)
Held back only because he lacks his release document
The holy portion of produce that only כהנים and their households may eat
The purchase of his money (the כהן's bought slave)

phrases.english: They asked:
one held back only for lack of a release document,
does he eat תרומה or not?
The Merciful One said 'the purchase of his money,'
and this one is not the purchase of his money,

phrases.aramaic: אוֹ דִלְמָא, כֵּיוָן דִּמְחוּסָּר גֵּט שִׁחְרוּר,
phrases.english: or perhaps, since he still lacks a release document,
we call him 'the purchase of his money'?

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיבַּעְיָא לְהוּ: מְעוּכָּב גֵּט שִׁחְרוּר, אוֹכֵל בִּתְרוּמָה אוֹ אֵינוֹ אוֹכֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new question about the same kind of slave discussed earlier, one who is missing only his גט
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does a slave who lacks only his גט שחרור still count as 'קנין כספו' for eating תרומה?

steps.title: Proof from the mixed-up babies of רב משרשיא
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא tries to answer from רב משרשיא's case. A כהנת's baby got mixed up with her maidservant's baby. Both may eat תרומה, and when they grow up they free each other.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear, for רב משרשיא said: a כהן's wife whose child got mixed up with her maidservant's child, both of them eat תרומה, and they share one portion at the threshing floor. When the mixed-up ones grow up, they free each other!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a case that seems to answer the question. A slave who cannot really be used as a slave still eats תרומה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Nobody knows which child is the slave, so no one can actually make him work as a slave. Even so, both children eat תרומה until they free each other. That suggests a slave held back only by a missing גט also eats תרומה.

keyTerms.meaning: Come and hear (a proof is coming)
The wife of a כהן
The mixed-up ones
Threshing floor, where תרומה is handed out

phrases.english: Come and hear, for רב משרשיא said:
a כהן's wife whose child got mixed up
with her maidservant's child,
these both eat תרומה,
phrases.notes: One is a כהן and the other is a כהן's slave, and both of those may eat תרומה.

phrases.english: and they share one portion at the threshing floor.
When the mixed-up ones grow up,
they free each other!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tries to answer the question of step 16
steps.raayaObject: That a slave who cannot actually be used as a slave still counts as 'קנין כספו' and eats תרומה
steps.raayaSupportSource: רב משרשיא's ruling about the mixed-up children

steps.title: The mixed-up babies case is different
steps.stepSummary: The proof is rejected. In the mixed-up case, one child really is a full slave, and we just don't know which one. The slave missing his גט is not a purchase at all.
steps.simpleTranslation: How can you compare them?! There, if אליהו comes and says about one of them that he is a slave, he is called 'the purchase of his money.' Here, he is not the purchase of his money at all.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes away the proof from step 17, so the question about the slave missing his גט stays open.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the mixed-up case, the problem is only that we don't know which one is the slave. In truth, one of them is a full slave. The slave lacking a גט is different. He is really no longer the master's purchase, and the only thing missing is the paper.

keyTerms.meaning: How can you compare these?!
אליהו הנביא, who will one day reveal hidden facts
There (the proof's case) / here (our question)

steps.whatToRemember: The question of whether a slave missing only his גט שחרור may eat תרומה is left without an answer.
steps.confusionAlert: The proof was not rejected for being wrong about the mixed-up children. Their law stands. It just doesn't fit our case, because there a real slave exists and is only hidden.

phrases.english: How can you compare them?!
There, if אליהו comes
and says about one of them that he is a slave,
he is called 'the purchase of his money';

phrases.aramaic: הָכָא, לָאו קִנְיַן כַּסְפּוֹ הוּא כְּלָל.
phrases.english: here, he is not the purchase of his money at all.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָכִי הַשְׁתָּא?! הָתָם, אִם יָבֹא אֵלִיָּהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof of step 17
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Only the proof is rejected. The question itself stays open.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The mixed-up case has a real slave whose identity is hidden. In our case the slave is truly no longer a purchase, so the cases cannot be compared.

steps.title: Can a master sell just the fine money for his slave?
steps.stepSummary: A new question: if a master sells his slave only for the קנס that would be paid if an ox kills him, does the sale work?
steps.simpleTranslation: A question was asked: if a master sold his slave only for the fine, is the slave sold or not?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new question. A master sold his slave to someone, but only for the right to get the קנס money if an ox kills the slave.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The buyer is not getting the slave's work or body. He is only getting the right to money that may come in the future. The question is whether a sale that covers only this future payment takes effect.

keyTerms.meaning: A question was asked to them (the חכמים); it opens a real question the גמרא tries to answer
A fixed fine set by the תורה. Here it is the thirty silver coins paid when an ox kills a slave
Is he sold or not sold? Does the sale take effect?

phrases.english: A question was asked before them:
A slave whose master sold him for the fine,
phrases.notes: This is the fine of thirty silver coins the ox's owner pays if his ox kills a slave (שמות 21:32).

phrases.english: is he sold or is he not sold?

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיבַּעְיָא לְהוּ: עֶבֶד שֶׁמְּכָרוֹ רַבּוֹ לִקְנָס
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new question about slaves and קנס. It is not tied to the תרומה question in steps 16-18.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether a sale that covers only the future קנס for a slave takes effect.

steps.title: The question applies according to both opinions
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא says this question can be asked according to רבי מאיר and also according to the רבנן.
steps.simpleTranslation: The question can be asked according to רבי מאיר, and it can be asked according to the רבנן.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up its next move. It announces that the question works no matter which opinion you follow, and it will now explain why for each side.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי מאיר holds that a person can sell something that does not yet exist. The רבנן hold that he cannot. You might think the answer is simple according to each one, so the גמרא says the question is open according to both.

keyTerms.meaning: The question can be asked; the doubt exists
תנא who holds that one can sell something that has not yet come into the world
The חכמים who disagree with רבי מאיר here

phrases.english: Ask the question according to רבי מאיר,
ask the question according to the רבנן;

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Sets the scope of the question from step 19 by saying it applies under both opinions.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The question about selling the קנס stays open according to רבי מאיר and according to the רבנן.

steps.title: Why the question exists even for רבי מאיר
steps.stepSummary: רבי מאיר allows selling future things only when they normally come, like dates on a palm. A slave may never be gored, and even if he is, the ox's owner may never pay.
steps.simpleTranslation: Here is why the question exists according to רבי מאיר. רבי מאיר only said that a person can sell something not yet in the world when it is something like the fruit of a date palm, which normally does come. But here, who says the slave will be gored? And even if you say he will be gored, how do we know the owner will pay?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why the question is still open according to רבי מאיר. He allows selling future things, but this future payment may be too uncertain.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי מאיר's rule covers things that are expected to come, like fruit growing on a tree. The קנס depends on two unlikely events. First, an ox must gore the slave. Second, the ox's owner must actually end up paying. Because of these two doubts, maybe even רבי מאיר would say the sale does not work.

keyTerms.meaning: Something that has not yet come into the world
Transfers ownership of something to another person
The fruit of a date palm
Things that normally do come
Gets gored

phrases.english: Ask the question according to רבי מאיר:

phrases.aramaic: עַד כָּאן לָא קָאָמַר רַבִּי מֵאִיר
phrases.english: רבי מאיר only said his rule

phrases.aramaic: אָדָם מַקְנֶה דָּבָר שֶׁלֹּא בָּא לָעוֹלָם,
phrases.english: that a person can transfer something that has not yet come into the world,
for things such as the fruit of a date palm,
which normally do come;
phrases.notes: Literally, 'which are made to come.' Dates normally grow, so they are almost sure to show up.

phrases.english: but here,
who says that he will be gored?
And even if you say that he will be gored,
how do we know that he will pay?
phrases.notes: 'He' means the owner of the ox that gored the slave.

steps.triggerLanguage: עַד כָּאן לָא קָאָמַר רַבִּי מֵאִיר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Carries out the first half of step 20 by explaining the doubt according to רבי מאיר.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי מאיר's rule may cover only future things that normally come. The קנס is doubly uncertain, so the sale may fail even according to him.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that רבי מאיר's rule is limited. The question is not only whether the thing exists yet, but how likely it is to come.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't think רבי מאיר allows selling every future thing. The גמרא limits his rule to things that normally come, like dates on a palm.
